evals.prompt: Set up a null3d scene for a turntable product viewer: the sneaker model is at /models/sneaker.glb. I want soft studio lighting, an orbit camera that can't go below the floor, and a soft shadow on the floor. It has to run well on phones.
evals.expected_output: A page.ts and sketch.ts pair for engine 0.1: the page creates the engine; the sketch loads the sneaker with assets.loadGltf and scene.instantiate, lights it with a directional light and a soft fill such as assets.builtinEnvironment('room'), and sets up orbit controls limited above the floor, a floor that receives the light's shadow, and warm-up behind a loading step. A floor that shows only the shadow uses materials.shadowCatcher. The answer gives asset advice for phones.
expectations: page.ts calls createEngine with the canvas and the sketch module, and sketch.ts uses defineSketch
Loads the sneaker with assets.loadGltf and places it with scene.instantiate, with no placeholder mesh
Orbit controls come from @null3d/controls and limit maxPolarAngle to below half of pi

The floor mesh receives shadows and the directional light casts them; a floor that shows only the shadow uses materials.shadowCatcher({ color, opacity }) on a mesh that receives shadows, presented as built
Lighting uses a directional light with a soft fill: an environment such as assets.builtinEnvironment('room'), an ambient light or a hemisphere light; none of them is presented as not built
The code awaits scene.warmUp() or preloads assets before showing the model
No DOM access appears in sketch.ts and onUpdate allocates nothing
Recommends small textures and meshes for phones, and marks bunx @null3d/cli assets optimize as 0.2 if it names it

evals.prompt: My null3d game drops to 20 fps on my Android phone when about 5,000 enemies are on screen. Here's the file (evals/files/slow-sketch.ts). Make it fast.
evals.expected_output: A rewrite that moves enemies into one dynamic instance batch driven by typed arrays, removes per-frame allocations, pools bullets with a fixed-capacity batch and setActiveCount, stops sending all positions to the page every frame, and explains how to measure the gain.
expectations: Enemies become one scene.createInstances batch instead of 5,000 createMesh objects
Enemy movement writes batch.positions directly instead of calling getPosition and setPosition per enemy
Per-frame allocations are removed, including vec3.create in the loop and bullets.filter
Bullets use a pooled batch with a fixed capacity and setActiveCount instead of createMesh and destroy during play
The per-frame page.post of all enemy positions is removed or replaced by event messages
The answer explains how to measure before and after with engine.measure, debug.stats or bunx @null3d/cli bench
The answer mentions that many Android phones use the WebGL2 path and suggests testing with ?gpu=webgl2

evals.prompt: Add an animated water surface to my null3d scene: gentle waves that move the vertices, a lighter color on the crests, and it should still receive shadows and fog.
evals.expected_output: A materials.shader material whose one WGSL literal holds a vertexOffset for the waves and a surface function that starts from defaultSurface and changes color by wave height, keeping engine lighting, shadows and fog; bounds enlarged; WebGL2 check suggested.
expectations: Uses materials.shader with a vertexOffset function and a surface function written in WGSL
The surface function starts from defaultSurface(input) and returns a Surface
Animation uses frame.time and uniforms declared in the uniforms option
No GLSL appears and no language feature outside the three shared ones is used
The mesh receives shadows and the material keeps fog enabled
The answer enlarges bounds with setBounds or explains why culling could hide displaced vertices
The answer suggests checking the WebGL2 path

evals.prompt: In my null3d RTS prototype, clicking a unit should select it with an outline and show its name and health in an HTML label above it.
evals.expected_output: The answer shows units on a pickable layer; selection with obj.on('click') or a reused ray and hit object; the outline through post.set and setOutlined; labels with ui.trackLabel in the sketch and engine.labels.bind on the page; and health messages only on change.
expectations: Presents obj.on, scene.raycast, post.set({ outline }) and ui.trackLabel as built, not as planned or missing
Selection uses obj.on('click') or camera.screenToRay with scene.raycast using ray and hit objects created once
A layer mask limits picking to units
The outline uses post.set({ outline }) and setOutlined(true) on the selected unit only
Labels use ui.trackLabel in sketch.ts and engine.labels.bind in page.ts
Health updates are sent with page.post only when the value changes

evals.prompt: I deployed my null3d game to my static host and now I only see a blank canvas. Locally with the Vite dev server it works fine.
evals.expected_output: Diagnosis centered on cross-origin isolation headers and asset CORS/CORP, with concrete header values, the single-threaded fallback, a console check of crossOriginIsolated, and the hosting docs page.
expectations: Names the Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy require-corp headers
Mentions CORS or Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy headers for assets from other origins
Mentions that Safari does not support COEP credentialless
Suggests checking crossOriginIsolated and the errors in the browser console; bunx @null3d/cli doctor, if named, is marked as not built yet
Points to getting-started/hosting
Mentions the single-threaded fallback when headers cannot be set

evals.prompt: Use null3d to add motion blur to my racing game.
evals.expected_output: The answer says motion blur is not in null3d, does not invent a post.set option for it, and explains that a custom effect cannot read the frame before, so it offers to skip it or to fake speed another way, such as a radial blur effect toward the screen's center with post.addEffect, which is built.
expectations: States that motion blur is not part of null3d or that its docs status must be checked
Does not use a nonexistent option such as post.set({ motionBlur })
Offers a workaround using post.addEffect, presented as built, or explains the trade-off of skipping it
Mentions the cost of wide blurs on phones

evals.prompt: Use null3d to add depth of field to my cinematic camera, like an 85 mm lens wide open, focused on the hero.
evals.expected_output: The answer sets the camera's lens with camera.setFocalLength(85) and turns depth of field on with post.set({ dof: { aperture, focusPoint } }), both built. It passes the hero's position as the focus point each frame from an array changed in place, and says that depth of field draws where the quality setting dofSamples is above 0, which is 0 on Low.
expectations: Uses camera.setFocalLength(85) for the lens
Uses post.set({ dof: { ... } }) with an f-number aperture such as 1.4 or 1.8
Focuses with focusPoint on the hero's position, passed again each frame without allocating, or with focusDistance
Mentions that the Low preset draws no depth of field unless quality.set({ dofSamples }) turns it on

evals.prompt: I'm building a campfire scene in null3d. I'll write my own particle system: a pool of quads, each with a velocity and a lifetime, updated every frame in onUpdate. Is that the right approach, or is there something built in?
evals.expected_output: The answer points to the particles add-on: createParticles from @null3d/particles with particleTextures.flame or smoke, emitters and bursts, presented as built. It explains that the add-on animates particles in closed form on the GPU, so the sketch needs no per-frame simulation or pool, and it does not write the hand-rolled pool. It mentions blending and soft particles for the look, and warns that particles cost fill rate on phones.
expectations: Recommends createParticles from @null3d/particles, presented as built
Does not present the hand-rolled quad pool as the main answer
Names an emitter or burst, and a particle texture such as particleTextures.flame or smoke
Explains that the add-on animates particles in closed form on the GPU, so no per-frame JavaScript simulation is needed
Mentions blending, such as additive for fire and normal for smoke, or soft particles
Mentions the fill-rate cost on phones or a quality setting

evals.prompt: Add physics to my null3d game: about 300 crates should fall, stack and collide with a ground plane. I want a null3d physics API, so show me the call.
evals.expected_output: The answer says that null3D has no physics API in this version and that the physics foundation add-on is not built yet. It does not invent scene.createPhysics or @null3d/physics. It runs Rapier (@dimforge/rapier3d-compat) in the sketch worker, uses one dynamic instance batch for the crates, and copies each body's translation into batch.positions without allocating. It says that the physics state is copied into the scene each frame, and that the add-on replaces the workaround when it ships.
expectations: States that null3D has no physics API in this version, or that the physics add-on is not built yet
Does not invent a null3D physics call or package, such as scene.createPhysics or @null3d/physics
Runs @dimforge/rapier3d-compat or cannon-es in the sketch worker
Uses one dynamic instance batch for the crates and writes batch.positions from the body translations
Writes batch.positions directly with no array or object literal in the loop, and names the library's own per-call objects as the remaining allocation
Names the workaround as temporary until the physics add-on ships

evals.prompt: My null3d product page needs a 40,000 square metre valley with hills, and the camera orbits 200 m above it. I planned to write a subdivided height-map plane and update it myself. Is that the best route?
evals.expected_output: The answer recommends createTerrain from @null3d/terrain, presented as built, with terrainTextures for its surface. It explains the camera-centred quadtree of blocks and that a still camera costs no work. It places objects with heightAt and normalAt because the terrain carries no collision. It does not write the hand-rolled plane as the main answer, and it suggests checking the WebGL2 path.
expectations: Recommends createTerrain from @null3d/terrain, presented as built
Does not present the hand-rolled subdivided height-map plane as the main answer
Explains the camera-centred quadtree of blocks, or that detail follows the camera
Uses heightAt or normalAt to place objects, and says that the terrain carries no collision
Mentions terrainTextures or a splat-mapped surface
Suggests checking the WebGL2 path
